nature-nbs-304.title: Rotational grazing: moving herds so pasture can rest
nature-nbs-304.text: A cow on a rotated pasture may produce less, yet the farm can come out ahead. Rotational grazing moves livestock between sections of pasture, called paddocks, so the rest of the pasture can recover. It usually yields less than intensive operations but needs fewer inputs, so net income per animal can be higher. More cows can graze each acre, giving more output per acre at less cost. Manure returns most nutrients, and swards with over 40% legumes need no commercial nitrogen. Some systems erode less and may cut emissions. Legume-rich pasture risks bloat, which can be fatal. And in 87% of experiments, plant production was equal or greater under continuous grazing, so scientists dispute its ecological edge. GPS collars can now automate rotations with virtual fences.

nature-nbs-263.title: Silvopasture: trees, grass and livestock together
nature-nbs-263.text: Under partial tree cover, near-ground air can be up to 7% cooler than in open pasture. Silvopasture combines trees, forage plants and grazing livestock on the same land so each benefits the others. It is a form of agroforestry that uses managed grazing. Selling tree crops, forage and livestock together can raise productivity and long-term income. Carbon uptake is lowest in open pasture, intermediate in silvopasture and highest in forest. Done correctly, it can count as a nature-based solution to climate change. But it needs heavy upfront investment and typically takes 3–6 years to give returns. Barriers include policy hurdles, land tenure, lack of knowledge and cultural change.

nature-nbs-243.title: Conservation agriculture: three rules for protecting farmland
nature-nbs-243.text: Farmers who stop tilling can save 30% to 40% of their time and labor. That is one draw of conservation agriculture, a system defined by the FAO that protects farmland and restores degraded land. It rests on three principles. First, minimal soil disturbance, such as no-till, keeps minerals in the soil and prevents erosion and water loss. Second, a permanent cover of mulch shields soil from rain and wind and builds organic matter. Third, diverse crop rotation breaks pest and weed cycles and improves water infiltration. The benefits come slowly: organic matter takes years to build, and early years can bring losses. Special planting equipment is costly, and livestock compete for crop residues.

nature-nbs-232.title: Farming's greenhouse gases: cows, fertilizer and cleared land
nature-nbs-232.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute 13%–21% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Some come directly from crops and livestock; others come indirectly, from clearing land for farms. Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of agriculture's direct emissions. Making and using nitrogen fertilizer alone contributes around 5% of all global emissions. Livestock production accounts for almost 60% of food-system emissions. Ruminants such as cows and sheep give off methane made by microbes in their guts.

nature-nbs-229.title: Climate-smart agriculture: three goals at once
nature-nbs-229.text: Rainfed farming makes up 80% of global agriculture, so shifting rainfall threatens many poor farmers in Asia and Africa. Climate-smart agriculture is a set of methods that try at once to adapt farming to climate change, raise yields for food security and cut farm emissions. The World Bank calls it practices that together boost productivity, build resilience and reduce greenhouse gases. The FAO stresses it is not a new set of practices but an approach fitted to local contexts. Examples include heat-tolerant varieties, mulching, boundary trees and suitable cattle housing. Carbon farming is one component. Farming, forestry and land use produce 13%–21% of global emissions. Yet no accepted standard defines it, and critics call the label {{ref:nature-nbs-075}} for big businesses.

nature-nbs-274.title: Biodiversity on farmland
nature-nbs-274.text: The FAO estimates more than 40% of Earth's land surface is used for agriculture, which makes habitat loss the main driver of biodiversity loss. Biodiversity in agriculture is the variety of living things on farmland. It falls as varied landscapes are lost and native plants give way to crops. Fallow land, grass margins and scrub strips add habitat variety, and smaller fields have been linked to more species. Diversity pays. In Asian rice, flowering strips beside fields cut insecticide spraying by 70% and raised yields by 5%, an economic advantage of 7.5%. Low crop diversity can increase pests and pesticide resistance.

nature-nbs-268.title: Fertilizer runoff: when nutrients escape the field
nature-nbs-268.text: At 1900 yield levels, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land. Fertilizers made that difference, but not all of them stay where they are spread. Fertilizer runoff is the loss of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized fields into water and air, where they pollute. Nitrate dissolves easily, so it runs off into rivers and lakes and leaches into groundwater. Above 10 mg/L in groundwater, nitrate can cause blue baby syndrome in infants. Phosphorus is the largest contributor to eutrophication, the overfeeding of waters with nutrients, especially in fresh water. Fertilization also releases nitrous oxide. It is a greenhouse gas, and it harms the ozone layer high in the stratosphere.

nature-nbs-241.title: Ecological farming: rebuilding what the land provides
nature-nbs-241.text: Ecological farming focuses on the environmental side of sustainable agriculture, using methods that rebuild ecosystem services. It aims to prevent erosion, improve water infiltration, store carbon as humus and raise biodiversity. Techniques include no-till farming, multispecies cover crops, strip cropping, terraces and shelter belts. It also values crop genetic diversity, which lowers the risks of single-crop fields that can be vulnerable to a changing climate.

nature-nbs-240.title: Land blending: a middle path between sparing and sharing
nature-nbs-240.text: If neither sparing nor sharing wins everywhere, why choose? Land blending is an in-between strategy that mixes the two to suit each landscape. It only recently emerged as a credible alternative. Research suggests it can reconcile conservation and farming while building resilience.

nature-nbs-242.title: Multifunctional agriculture: farms produce more than food
nature-nbs-242.text: A farm turns out more than food and fiber. Multifunctional agriculture is the view that farming also manages renewable resources, conserves landscapes and supports biodiversity. It is a farm-centered lens that treats these functions as outputs of farming. The rival ecosystem-services lens starts instead from the benefits nature gives people, such as pollination, soil formation and nutrient cycling.

nature-nbs-279.title: The rotation effect: why rotated crops yield more
nature-nbs-279.text: Rotated crops tend to out-yield crops grown alone year after year. That yield gain is called the rotation effect. It arises mainly from relieving the problems of growing one crop repeatedly: plants get better nutrition, face less pest and weed stress, and grow in better-structured soil.

nature-nbs-277.title: The three-field system of medieval Europe
nature-nbs-277.text: Between the 9th and 11th centuries, European farmers moved from a two-field system to a three-field one. Land was divided into autumn crops, spring crops and a fallow field, rotated each year. Two thirds of the land was planted instead of half. The legume crops improved people's nutrition. The system lasted until the 20th century.

nature-nbs-278.title: Four-field rotation: turnips, clover and year-round livestock
nature-nbs-278.text: In the 18th century, a new rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover let farmers keep livestock all year. Charles Townshend popularized this four-field rotation. It became a key development of the British Agricultural Revolution, building on the older {{ref:nature-nbs-277}}.

nature-nbs-248.title: Alley cropping: crops in strips between tree rows
nature-nbs-248.text: Alley cropping grows strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges. The trees feed the crop: pruned leaves are spread over it to supply nutrients. The hedges also block wind, reduce erosion and suppress weeds with their mulch and shade.

nature-nbs-252.title: Forest farming: specialty crops under the canopy
nature-nbs-252.text: Forest farming grows high-value specialty crops under a forest canopy managed to give the right shade and habitat. It ranges from planting crops under timber trees to adjusting existing stands so their plants sell better. In 1929 J. Russell Smith's book Tree Crops argued that tree crops could replace cereals in animal feed and protect the environment.

nature-nbs-253.title: Forest gardens: food grown in woodland layers
nature-nbs-253.text: Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest form of land use. They produce food with little upkeep, modeled on woodland, with layers of fruit and nut trees, shrubs, herbs, vines and perennial vegetables. They remain common in the tropics as home gardens and are a significant source of income and food security there. Robert Hart coined the term in the 1980s and adapted the idea to the UK's temperate climate.

nature-nbs-249.title: Shade-grown crops: farming beneath the trees
nature-nbs-249.text: Some crops do better out of full sun. Shade-grown crops are deliberately grown beneath a canopy of trees. Shade-grown coffee is the best-known example. Shading cuts weeding costs and improves the quality of the coffee.

nature-nbs-254.title: Urban agroforestry: trees and crops in the city
nature-nbs-254.text: Agroforestry on rooftop gardens can cut energy demand for cooling by up to 20%. Urban agroforestry applies the same idea in towns, combining trees, shrubs and crops in gardens, parks and streets. Its main constraint is cost. Urban land is valuable, so the opportunity cost of giving it to trees, the value of the best use forgone, is high.

nature-nbs-251.title: Windbreaks: tree rows that shelter crops
nature-nbs-251.text: Wind dries crops and knocks them flat. Windbreaks are rows of trees or shrubs planted to slow the wind over and around fields. They raise yields by reducing crop drying and stopping plants from being blown over. The USDA lists them as one of five temperate agroforestry practices.

nature-nbs-311.title: Testing soil health
nature-nbs-311.text: Soil health testing measures a soil's physical, chemical and biological condition against benchmarks of healthy function. Benchmarks include CO2 release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium. Many labs resist the new biological tests. Fertility testing rests on models of how crops respond, and soil health has no equivalent yet.

nature-nbs-306.title: Contour plowing: furrows that follow the hill
nature-nbs-306.text: Contour plowing can raise crop yields by 10 to 50 percent, partly by keeping soil in place. Farmers plow furrows along a slope's contour lines so the furrows stay level and slow runoff. The idea is old: the ancient Phoenicians used it on slopes of two to ten percent.

nature-nbs-308.title: Keyline design: shaping a whole watershed
nature-nbs-308.text: Keyline design extends contour plowing from one field to a whole watershed. It shapes contour lines around the entire drainage basin so water spreads and soaks in. It is used on regenerative farms alongside diverse livestock and crop production.

nature-nbs-309.title: Managing salt in farm soils
nature-nbs-309.text: Salinity affects about one third of the earth's arable land. Salt breaks down soil structure and causes infertility, and it mainly builds up from irrigating with salty water. After the 1970 Aswan Dam, a raised water table salinized soils in Egypt. Managing salinity means preventing and reducing this build-up. Salt-tolerant plants such as saltbush can lower water tables and slow surface salt build-up.

nature-nbs-307.title: Terrace farming: steps cut into hillsides
nature-nbs-307.text: A steep hill can be farmed if it is cut into steps. Terrace farming carves a hillside into a series of nearly level platforms for crops. Terraces slow the rapid runoff of irrigation water, which keeps soil from washing away. They are more common on small farms.

nature-nbs-259.title: Holistic planned grazing: imitating wild herds
nature-nbs-259.text: In a TED talk, Allan Savory claimed his grazing method could bring carbon dioxide back to pre-industrial levels in 40 years. Critics reject this. Holistic planned grazing moves herds constantly between fields to imitate wild herds. Supporters say trampling restores soil, stimulates regrowth and raises soil carbon and water infiltration. But a meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found it did no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and biomass. The evidence on its carbon benefits is mixed.

nature-nbs-227.title: Bamboo as a carbon crop
nature-nbs-227.text: Bamboo grows fast, and some farmers plant it to store carbon. A bamboo forest holds less total carbon than most mature forests. It can match rubber plantations and orchards, though, and beats agroforests, palm oil plantations and grasslands. Bamboo takes up carbon faster than mature forests, but only when new or actively managed.
